lines: Thunder shook the stonecutter so hard loose stones rattled in the wall, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked walls, steps, and cracked blocks after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the stonecutter, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the doorframes twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have doorframes to set right.
Rain found a gap above the workshop that yesterday looked harmless.
We kept away from the tall tower until the clouds moved east.
A bolt struck close enough to leave the stone warm.
The children stayed in the cellar while we watched the doors.
Water filled the lower lane faster than the drain could carry it.
I found fresh mortar on the floor beneath a crack that was not there this morning.
The bell was useless under that noise, so we sent word from house to house.
Every chimney needs checking before anyone lights a fire tonight.
The old wall leaned through the storm and somehow settled back straight.
We moved two families out of the house beside the struck tree.
The worst has passed, but nobody goes near the wet scaffolding yet.
I marked the damaged corners before the rain could hide them.
The village is standing. A few roofs will need honest work tomorrow.
Lightning scares people quickly. Cracked stone waits until later.
Next time those clouds gather, I am clearing the square before the first strike.
I checked wooden beams set into stone for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and <dark_gray><wavy>fear</wavy></dark_gray>.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the stonecutter after.
The stonecutter can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the stonecutter, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the stonecutter, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
I knocked loose plaster away so we could find the hot beam behind it.
One roof is gone, but the family under it is safe.
The bucket line reached from the well to the far end of the square.
We pulled the hay carts away before the sparks reached them.
A wall can survive fire and still be too weak to trust.
I burned my sleeve clearing rubble from the doorway.
The golem carried a fallen beam like it weighed nothing.
We soaked the neighboring roofs while the wind pushed embers across them.
The flames are out. The stones underneath are still hot enough to hurt.
I am checking every chimney for cracks before night.
Nobody went back for furniture. That choice saved time we did not have.
The workshop tools are wet, and I am glad the water reached them.
We found the missing child coughing behind the fountain wall.
Tomorrow we rebuild what burned. Tonight we watch the ashes.
People first, roofs second, stone last. That was the right order.
During a raid, the stonecutter can sit silent. Who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the stonecutter still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before walls, steps, and cracked blocks. That's the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the stonecutter and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the stonecutter, I saw fear cross the square. Then I saw courage get there first.
A crossbow bolt chipped the arch above my head.
The west wall bought enough time to move the children inside.
One raider climbed the rubble and met the iron golem at the top.
I carried blocks to the breach while others held the lane.
The square looked lost for a moment, then everyone found their nerve.
They broke the gate but never reached the beds behind it.
Two houses took damage when the fighting crossed the road.
I saw neighbors who never agree stand shoulder to shoulder.
The last horn stopped before dawn, but nobody trusted the quiet.
We marked every damaged wall before anyone started celebrating.
The wounded are inside. Give the healer room to work.
I found my hammer in the road beside a broken banner.
The village held because people did, not because stone is brave.
We will build the gate stronger after everyone has slept.
The raiders are gone. Keep watch until the scouts return.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the stonecutter first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the wall with the missing block and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the stonecutter enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a stack of spare stone between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the stonecutter, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
Something struck the workshop shutters hard enough to bend the hinges.
We moved the children into the stone storehouse before the second alarm.
An arrow came through the window and buried itself in the mortar shelf.
The golem stood at the crossroads until sunrise.
Every shadow looked alive after the first attack.
I patched one doorway with blocks that do not match and do not need to.
The torch line ended too close to the fields. We are extending it today.
Nobody slept after the scratching started at the doors.
We found tracks circling three houses in the morning.
The old wall kept the monsters in the open where the watch could see them.
One villager is missing a window, but no one is missing from the count.
Tonight we put two watchers by the gate instead of one.
The last groan faded before the birds started.
I am checking every door bar while there is still daylight.
We made it to morning. The repairs begin before the next sunset.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand from the mortar lines.
I checked walls, steps, and cracked blocks, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the stonecutter, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a mason which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the stonecutter, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
One doorway packed shut before the family inside could open it.
We covered our faces and counted voices when we could not count heads.
The grit stripped fresh mortar from the exposed wall.
I found a roof tile in the square that belongs to no roof nearby.
Every hinge needs cleaning before it decides to stay closed.
The western wall turned the worst of the wind away from the homes.
A child followed the guide rope back with both eyes shut.
The storm filled the workshop with a dune no broom deserves.
We kept the water jars sealed and the doors braced.
The bell was the only landmark anyone could hear.
One chimney cracked when the wind threw debris against it.
The air is clearer now, but keep a cloth over your mouth.
I marked the buried corners so nobody trips while digging out.
No one was lost. We are finding the paths one doorstep at a time.
I will be clearing sand from the stonecutter for a week.
The stonecutter can sit silent. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the stonecutter found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the stonecutter. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing ice off the steps and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the stonecutter. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
One roof bowed under the weight and needed every shovel in the lane.
We tied a rope between the bell and the nearest houses.
The chimney draw is poor in this weather. Check every room for smoke.
I raised the well marker before the drift swallowed it.
No one crosses the square alone until the whiteout lifts.
The mortar will not set in this cold, so the broken wall is braced for now.
We cleared the bakery first. Warm bread keeps shovel hands moving.
The wind erased our tracks almost as soon as we made them.
I found ice inside a crack that was dry yesterday.
Every spare blanket went to someone who needed it.
The snow stopped before dawn, but the roofs are still heavy.
I am checking on anyone who stopped complaining about the cold.
The village is quiet because everyone is indoors and listening.
When the thaw comes, the foundations will need another inspection.
Nobody froze alone. That matters more than the work waiting outside.
